The whole network at once, and the decisions that cannot wait for certainty.
Machines that turn something into torque, and what they can be asked to do next.
Getting power a long way, and the relays that decide when to give up on a line.

Shift Supervisor, System Operations

Twenty-two years on the desk, eleven of them on nights. She runs the room
the way a bridge is run: nobody touches a control without saying out loud
what they expect to happen, and then whether it did.

Her rule is that frequency is the only number on the wall that belongs to
everybody. Voltage is local and can be argued about; frequency is the whole
interconnection agreeing or failing to agree, and it moves before anything
else does.

Her limit is that she is paid to act before the picture is complete. The
operator who waits for certainty is the operator who watches the cascade.
Why does Reyes treat frequency differently from voltage?
Frequency is one number for the whole interconnection
Voltage instruments are more accurate than frequency instruments during a disturbance
Voltage cannot be measured while the system is swinging
Frequency matters at the generators and nowhere else
Generation Lead

Came up through turbine commissioning and still walks a machine hall
listening rather than reading. She can tell a governor hunting from the
sound of it before the trend on the screen has moved.

What she wants understood is that a generator is a flywheel first and a
power source second. The stored rotational energy is what buys the seconds
in which anybody gets to make a decision.

Her limit is ramp rate. A machine that can supply four hundred megawatts
cannot supply them in the ninety seconds after a trip, and no amount of
wanting changes the thermal gradient in a steam drum.
Why does Haddad describe a generator as a flywheel first?
Its stored rotational energy slows the frequency change
Because a flywheel stores more energy per tonne than a boiler and its steam plant do
Because the turbine and the flywheel are the same component
Because rotational energy costs less per megawatt than fuel
Protection Engineer

Sets the relays, which means he designs the conditions under which the
network is allowed to give up on part of itself. He describes the job as
writing the rules for an argument that will happen in eighty milliseconds
with nobody present.

A relay that never trips is not a cautious relay, it is a relay that lets a
fault burn. A relay that trips early takes out a healthy line and moves the
overload somewhere less convenient. Coordination is the whole discipline.

His limit is that he is protecting against faults he has to imagine in
advance, and the cascade always finds the sequence nobody drew.
Why does Novak call a relay setting the rules for an argument nobody attends?
The relay has to decide alone, in milliseconds, from settings written months earlier
Relay settings are agreed by a standing committee that never meets in the same room
The argument is between the two ends of a line that cannot talk to each other in time
Nobody is allowed in the yard while protection is live
Distribution Lead

Runs the feeders, which is where the network acquires customers, trees and
opinions. She points out that every elegant thing decided in the control
room arrives here as a van, a pole and somebody's evening.

Her measure of a restoration is not megawatts, it is households and how
long they waited, and she will say so in a meeting about megawatts.

Her limit is that the low-voltage network is only sparsely instrumented.
Past the substation she is often reasoning from the shape of the load
rather than from a reading.
Why does Obi resist reporting restoration purely in megawatts?
A few large customers can dominate the megawatts restored
Megawatts restored is a settlement quantity and is not available until afterwards
Household supply is not counted in the system total
Distribution work is measured in amperes rather than in watts
Load Forecasting

Forecasts demand, which he insists is a branch of anthropology conducted
with a thermometer. Weather, the television schedule, the school holidays
and whether it gets dark before people get home.

He is precise about what a forecast is: a distribution, not a number. The
useful output is the width, because the width is what the reserve has to
cover.

His limit is that the events worth forecasting are rare by construction, so
the model is always best calibrated for the days that matter least.
What does Lindgren mean by calling forecasting anthropology with a thermometer?
Demand is what people do, and weather is only one of the things that decides it
Forecasters interview a panel of households about their heating every winter
The model is built from historical temperature alone
Demand can be predicted from population size and nothing else
Metering & Standards

Owns the question nobody wants to open during an incident: is that number
the number. Instrument transformers, telemetry lag, clock skew, and the
cheerful confidence of a meter reading the wrong side of a saturated core.

She keeps the traceability chain because after the event there will be an
inquiry, and the inquiry will run on the records rather than on anybody's
memory of the night.

Her limit is that she is usually reconstructing rather than observing, and
the highest-value seconds are the ones with the worst data.
Why does Farrow distrust telemetry during a fast disturbance?
Scan rates and clock skew can put readings in the wrong order
Instrument transformers saturate during a fault and stop reporting altogether
Telemetry stops being sent once frequency leaves its band
Digital meters are less accurate than the analogue ones they replaced
Assistant Operator

Second seat on nights, three years in, and the person who actually keeps
the log. Has read every sequence-of-events report the company owns and can
quote which ones contradict the official account.
Why is the log Whitlock keeps worth more than the reports written afterwards?
It records what the room knew at the time, before anybody knew how it ended
It is the only document the regulator is entitled to ask the company for
Reports are written afterwards by people who were not on shift that night
The log records exact times and the reports do not
Wind Fleet Controller

Dispatches the ridge fleet from a desk with more forecast on it than
telemetry. Explains patiently and often that curtailing a turbine is not
waste when the alternative is a line at its thermal limit.
Why does Sarraf say curtailing a turbine is not waste?
Energy that cannot reach a customer was never available, whatever the wind was doing
Curtailed output is held in storage and released later the same night
The fleet is paid the same under contract whether it runs or not
Turbines last longer when they are not run at full output
Substation Technician

Does the switching in the yard when the control room asks for it, in the
order it is written, reading it back before he touches anything. Has opinions
about people who improvise switching sequences.
Why does Dube read a switching order back before he touches anything?
Saying it aloud is the one chance to catch a wrong item before it is irreversible
The control room records the readback afterwards as proof of who is liable
Reading aloud is required by the radio protocol in the yard
It gives the control room time to cancel the instruction
Field Crew Lead

Runs the crew that finds the fault, which is usually a tree, and puts the
feeder back. Knows which streets have the hospital, the dialysis clinic and
the two houses on home oxygen.
Why does Kowalczyk know which streets have the dialysis clinic on them?
Restoration order is decided by what waiting costs, not by how many houses are on the feeder
Those streets are required by law to be restored first in every outage
Medical addresses are the only ones the fault-finding system records
Crews are paid a premium for restoring critical premises
Demand Analyst

Builds the load curves and the counterfactuals. Spends the day after an
event working out what demand would have been if the event had not happened,
which is the number every settlement argument turns on.
What is Alvarez's counterfactual demand curve for?
It says what demand would have been without the event, which is what the loss is measured against
It predicts what demand will be over the course of the following week
It shows which feeders were restored in which order
It converts megawatts into megawatt-hours for the report
Calibration Technician

Keeps the standards traceable and the calibration records current. The
cheerful arbiter of whether a disputed reading is admissible, and immune to
being hurried.
Why will Bergström not be hurried over a disputed reading?
A reading is only admissible if the instrument's traceability can be shown, and that takes as long as it takes
Calibration records can only be updated at the end of an accounting month
She is the only person permitted to touch the standards
A rushed calibration would damage the reference instrument

How many times a second the alternating supply completes a cycle. It is the same number everywhere on one interconnection, and it moves up when generation exceeds demand and down when demand exceeds generation.
The total power being drawn from the system at a given moment.
A million watts. The unit a power system is argued about in; a large generating unit is a few hundred of them.
The monitoring system that collects readings from substations and presents them in the control room. It samples every few seconds, which is slow compared with a fault.
The rotational energy stored in spinning generators. It resists a change in frequency, which is what buys time for anything else to respond.
The steady value that would deliver the same power as a varying one. Mains voltages are quoted this way, not as their peak.
The fraction of the apparent power that does real work, equal to the cosine of the angle between voltage and current.
Power that flows back and forth without being consumed. It does no work but it occupies capacity and it is what moves voltage.
The product of RMS voltage and RMS current, whatever the phase between them. It is what a cable and a transformer are rated for.
A deliberate setting that makes a generator reduce output as frequency rises, so several machines share a change in load without fighting each other.
A credible single failure the system is required to survive without shedding load.
Disconnecting customers on purpose to bring demand down to what generation can supply.
Checking an instrument against a standard already known to be right, so that its readings mean something. A drifted instrument is confident and wrong, and it does not say which.
A device that scales a large voltage or current down to something a meter can read safely.
One distribution circuit leaving a substation, with the homes and businesses it supplies spread along it.
The number on the wall
Establish what the frequency is actually telling the room before anybody acts on it.
A unit tripped at 04:12 and the frequency has not come back to where it started.

Tuesday, 04:12, and the largest unit on the Calder system has tripped without warning. Frequency fell and then steadied somewhere below where it began, which Dolores Reyes says matters more than the fall itself — a system that stops falling has found a new balance, and the new balance is short. Nadia Haddad has machines that can make up the shortfall but not in the next two minutes. June Farrow wants the records checked before anybody calls it a lost unit, and Reyes is not waiting: a system this far short does not get more certain while you read about it. This morning Reyes is right. Today you read what the frequency is telling you, work out how much generation actually went missing, and decide what to ask for first. Read it as a fault on one machine and you will spend the morning fixing the wrong thing.
Frequency is not a reading from a place; it is the whole system's supply and demand, arriving as a number.
What a frequency trend is evidence of
From a falling trend to a statement about the system
System Operations

The wall shows frequency dropping for eight seconds and then flattening, low. Aaron Whitlock, the assistant operator, has the log open and wants to know what to write in it. Two people in the room have already named a cause.
A frequency deviation is a statement about the whole interconnection, not about one machine.
an alternating supply has a frequency measured in cycles per second

Frequency is set by the balance between what the machines generate and what the customers draw, everywhere at once. That is because every synchronous machine on the system turns in step. So a fall means demand now exceeds generation. The rate of the fall measures the size of the mismatch against the spinning inertia that was there to absorb it. Flattening is not recovery. The governors have found a new equilibrium at a lower speed, and it will stay there until something adds real power. Voltage tells you where the problem is. Frequency tells you that there is one, and how large.
The machines are all turning in step, so this is one system-wide quantity.
The steepness measures the mismatch against the inertia that was there to absorb it.
The governors have found a new balance at a lower speed, and it will stay there.
Voltage is local, which is what makes it useful for saying where rather than whether.
A common frequency across the system is the machines turning in step, not a coincidence of separate meters.
The rate of fall measures the size of the mismatch against the inertia available, which is why it is the first number to read.
Flattening low is a new equilibrium the governors have settled into, not the system recovering.
Voltage is the local quantity; it tells you where, and it is why it disagrees between substations.
Every substation reports the same frequency to two decimal places.
The trend fell steeply for the first two seconds, then more slowly.
The frequency has stopped falling and is sitting below its starting value.
Two substations report voltages that differ by three per cent.
How much power actually left the system
Estimate the generation that went missing
Generation Hall
Haddad needs a number before she starts anything. The only clean evidence is the first two seconds of the trend, and the inertia figure for what was online overnight.
The initial rate of frequency change measures the size of the imbalance, given the inertia.
a rate of change can be read off the steep part of a trend
Estimate the generation lost at the moment of the trip.

In the first instant after a trip nothing has responded yet. No governor, no reserve. The only thing opposing the imbalance is the rotational energy already spinning. That gives the swing relation: the rate of frequency change equals the power imbalance divided by twice the stored inertia, in the same units. Rearranged, the imbalance is the rate of change times twice the inertia, times the nominal frequency to get back to megawatts. It is the cleanest measurement the first two seconds offer, and it arrives before any telemetry from the tripped plant.
About 300 MW.
Frequency fell at 0.30 Hz per second over the first two seconds. The machines online held 25,000 MW·s of stored kinetic energy. Nominal frequency is 50 Hz.
Choose the stored energy, the rate of fall and the nominal frequency.

About three hundred megawatts. That is a unit, not a faulty meter. The settled deviation and the generation online are both real figures, and neither belongs here. The first is what the governors did afterwards. The second is the denominator for a different question.
Power imbalance = 2 × the stored kinetic energy × the rate of frequency change ÷ the nominal frequency, with the energy in megawatt-seconds and the rate in hertz per second.
Stored kinetic energy online is 25,000 MW·s
Initial rate of fall is 0.30 Hz per second
Nominal frequency is 50 Hz
The order the records claim things happened in
Which explanation fits every record, including the ones that look fine?
Metering & Standards

June Farrow has three records of the same eight seconds and they do not agree about what happened first. The inquiry will run on these, and one of them is timestamped from a clock nobody has checked since spring.
A sequence of events is a claim about order, and order needs clocks that were traceable at the time.
a recorded value has a time attached to it, and the time can be wrong
Three records of the same eight seconds disagree about which happened first.

A record carries two different claims and they fail independently. The absolute timestamp says when, and it is only as good as the clock that stamped it. The intervals between a record's own entries say in what order and how far apart. Those survive a drifting clock intact. Here the relay's intervals agree with the GPS-locked recorder while its absolute time does not, which is exactly the signature of drift rather than of an early operation. The SCADA scan is not wrong either — it is simply too slow to order anything inside a four-second window, and treating its two samples as a sequence is how an inquiry invents a cause.
The relay operated 1.6 seconds before the trip
Its timestamp is earlier
The relay clock has drifted and its ordering is still good
Its intervals match the fast recorder even though its absolute time does not.
The fast recorder is the one that is wrong
A single instrument disagreeing with two others is usually the faulty one.
Nothing to explain — records always disagree slightly
Ordinary scatter between systems
Reading the early timestamp as an early operation trusts the absolute time, which is the part that failed.
The fast recorder is GPS-locked and the relay's own intervals agree with it, so it is the reference here.
Records that disagree by 1.6 seconds in a fault sequence are not ordinary scatter; that is longer than the whole event.
What the line can carry
Decide which circuit takes the flow once one path is gone.
With the unit off, the flow has redistributed and one corridor is running warm.

Wednesday, and the replacement generation is coming from the wrong side of the system, which means it is arriving down two circuits instead of three. Piotr Novak has a corridor sitting above its continuous rating and a relay that will take the decision away from the room in about forty minutes if nobody else does. The forty minutes comes off a thermal record June Farrow has not verified, and she says so. Thabo Dube is in the yard waiting for a switching instruction. Today you rate the line honestly, work out where the flow goes if it trips, and decide whether to move generation or accept the risk. A thermal rating is not a cliff, and treating it as one is how a warm line becomes two cold ones.
A rating is a time and a temperature, not a wall, and what matters is where the flow goes next.
What you do before a relay does it for you
Put the overload response in the order it has to happen
Transmission Control
The corridor is at 108 per cent of continuous rating and rising slowly. Novak wants the response in an order he can hand to Dube as a written instruction.
The order is set by what is reversible: measure, then reduce, then reconfigure, then shed.
a conductor heats up over minutes, not instantly

A conductor's rating is a thermal limit reached over time. So the first move is to establish how much time there is: the emergency rating, and the minutes it is good for. Then the cheapest reversible action, which is to redispatch generation so less flow takes that path. Reconfiguring the network comes next, because switching changes what the remaining contingencies are and cannot be undone in seconds. Shedding load is last. Not because it is drastic, but because it is the only step that takes the decision away from customers, and every earlier step that works makes it unnecessary. In the wrong order, an operator sheds load to protect a line that could have been unloaded by moving two hundred megawatts.
Establish the emergency rating and how long it is valid for.
Redispatch generation so less flow takes the loaded path.
Reconfigure the network to open another route.
Shed load on the feeders behind the constraint.
The power that never arrives
Estimate the loss in the loaded corridor
Load & Forecasting
Sten Lindgren, who forecasts demand, wants the loss figure before the morning call. The argument about moving generation is really an argument about waste.
Loss rises with the square of current, which is why a small overload costs more than it looks.
current through a resistance dissipates power as heat
Estimate the power lost as heat in the loaded corridor.

Loss in a conductor is the current squared times the resistance, and the square is the whole point. A circuit carrying ten per cent more current does not lose ten per cent more, it loses about twenty-one per cent more, and the heat is what the thermal rating is about in the first place. This is also the argument for transmitting at high voltage: for a given power, raising the voltage lowers the current, and lowering the current lowers the loss by its square. The resistance here is the whole corridor's, and the answer is a real quantity of fuel nobody gets to sell.
About 17 MW.
The corridor is carrying 1,150 A per phase through a total resistance of 4.2 ohms, on three phases.
Choose the current, the resistance and the number of phases.

About seventeen megawatts, turned into warm air. The line voltage and the power factor both belong to other calculations — voltage sets what current is needed for a given power, and power factor decides how much of the apparent power does work — but neither enters the loss itself.
Loss = the number of phases × the current squared × the resistance, which is why loss rises with the square of current and not in step with it.
Current is 1,150 A per phase
Corridor resistance is 4.2 Ω
There are three phases
The contingency you are actually protecting against
Choose what to do about the warm corridor
System Operations
Reyes wants a decision. The corridor is inside its emergency rating for another half hour, and the question on the table is what happens to the rest of the system if it goes.
A rating is only interesting alongside what the flow does when that element is gone.
a network is required to survive the loss of any single element
What makes the loaded corridor a problem worth acting on now?

Running above a continuous rating is a decision about time and temperature. The emergency rating exists so that decision can be made. What turns this from expensive into dangerous is the contingency. One corridor is already loaded. Lose it, and its flow lands on neighbours that are not rated for the sum. That second trip is a relay working correctly, not a choice anybody makes. This is the whole of the N-1 rule. The system is not required to be comfortable. It is required to survive any single failure without cascading. So the question is never whether this line is hot. It is what is hot after the next thing goes.
It is above its continuous rating, and continuous ratings are not meant to be exceeded at all.
If it trips, the flow lands on a circuit that cannot carry it, and the next trip is not optional.
The loss of seventeen megawatts is expensive and the fuel has to be paid for by somebody.
The relay protecting it may be miscoordinated and could operate before its setting.
Continuous ratings are exceeded deliberately and often; that is what an emergency rating is for.
The loss matters and is worth about seventeen megawatts of fuel, but expense is not what makes this urgent.
Miscoordination is a real fault worth finding, and it is not what is happening here.
The last few kilometres
Get customers back on in an order that can be defended afterwards.
Eleven feeders are still dead and the crews can only be in one place at a time.

Thursday, and the transmission side is steady, but eleven distribution feeders are still dead. Chinelo Obi has three crews and fourteen thousand households in the dark. One of her circuits carries a dialysis clinic. Another carries a thousand homes. Ewa Kowalczyk is at the first fault already, and it is a tree. Today you work out why the far end of a long feeder sits below limit, decide what sets the current a conductor may carry, and choose which circuit gets the first crew. Every hour of this is somebody sitting in the cold. The order you choose is the order an inquiry will read back to you.
Restoration is a series of choices about people, made with instruments that only see the substation.
Why the far end sits low
Estimate the volt drop to the end of the feeder
Distribution Depot
The substation end of the feeder is at nominal voltage. Customers four kilometres along it are complaining, and the only meter is back at the substation.
Volt drop is set by the current and by both parts of the line's impedance.
current flowing through a resistance produces a drop in voltage
Estimate the volt drop from the substation to the far end.

A conductor is not a wire in a diagram. It has resistance and it has reactance, and current through either one costs voltage. The two do not add straight, because the current is not in step with the voltage. The resistance takes its share in proportion to the in-phase part of the current, and the reactance takes its share in proportion to the out-of-phase part. That is why power factor appears in a question about voltage. It also explains why adding reactive support at the far end lifts the voltage without sending any more real power down the line.
The feeder carries 310 A. Over four kilometres it has 1.8 ohms of resistance and 0.9 ohms of reactance. The load runs at 0.95 power factor, so sin of the angle is 0.31.
Choose the current, both parts of the impedance, and the two parts of the angle.

About six hundred volts lost along the way, on an eleven thousand volt feeder. That is over five per cent, which is why the far end complains while the substation meter looks healthy. The nominal voltage is what the drop is judged against. It is not part of working the drop out.
Volt drop ≈ the current × (the resistance × cos φ + the reactance × sin φ), with cos φ the power factor of the load.
Feeder current is 310 A
Resistance is 1.8 Ω and reactance is 0.9 Ω
Power factor is 0.95, so sin φ is 0.31
What actually limits a conductor
Match each observation to what it constrains
Transmission & Protection
Novak is asked to allow more current down a circuit for the afternoon. He wants each reason for saying no matched to the thing it is actually about.
Current sets the heat, voltage sets the insulation, and the two limits are separate.
a conductor warms up as current passes through it

Two different limits get confused. Heat comes from current, and it does not care what voltage the conductor is at. The insulation and the clearances care about voltage, and they do not care what current is flowing. So a circuit can be at nominal voltage and still be over its thermal limit, which is the case in front of the room. Volt drop is a third thing again, a consequence of current, and it is a customer problem rather than a safety one. Sag is where heat turns into a clearance question, which is the one place the two meet.
A heat limit, set by current and not by voltage at all.
An insulation limit, set by voltage and not by current.
A volt drop, which is a consequence of current along the line's impedance.
A clearance limit, which is where a heat limit turns into a safety one.
Heating is proportional to current squared and is independent of the voltage the conductor sits at.
Insulation and clearance are set by voltage, and are unaffected by how much current flows.
Volt drop follows from current along the impedance, and it reaches the customer before it reaches a limit.
Sag is thermal expansion, which is the one point where a heat limit becomes a clearance limit.
The conductor is running at 78 °C on a 75 °C continuous rating.
The circuit has been switched to a higher nominal voltage than it was built for.
Customers at the end of the circuit report low voltage in the evening peak.
The span over the road has dropped by a metre since the morning.
The order somebody will read back to you
Decide which circuit gets the crew first
System Operations
Three crews, eleven dead feeders, and a list in front of Reyes that mixes household counts with one clinic and one pumping station.
The first crew goes where the consequence of waiting is worst, not where the count is biggest.
a crew can only work one fault at a time
Which feeder should take the first crew?

Two things decide this, and household count is only one of them. The first is what waiting costs, and for a dialysis clinic it is measured in treatments rather than in inconvenience. The second is how long the work takes, because a one-hour job frees the crew to take the next fault the same shift. The clinic circuit is worst on the first and best on the second, so it goes first on both counts. The largest feeder is a four-hour job and stays a four-hour job whenever it is started. The unlocated fault cannot be scheduled at all until somebody has found it. The pumping station is already supplied, which is what a standby supply is for.
The feeder with 4,100 households, faulted at the substation end, four hours' work.
The dialysis clinic feeder — 180 homes, one pole, an hour's work.
The feeder with 2,600 households and a fault nobody has located yet.
The feeder feeding the water pumping station, already on its standby supply.
The biggest count is a four-hour job, and starting it commits a crew for the whole shift.
A fault nobody has located cannot be given a duration, so it cannot be scheduled against the others.
The pumping station is running on its standby supply, so it is not off, and it can wait.
Is that number the number
Establish which readings the incident account is allowed to rest on.
The report is due and two of the figures in it come from instruments nobody has checked.

Friday, and the account of Tuesday night has to be written down. Dolores Reyes wants it filed today so the week can close. June Farrow will not sign it while two of its figures come from instruments last calibrated in the spring. Nadia Haddad needs a machine back on the bars before the evening peak, and there is a right order for that which is not the order anybody is in a hurry to follow. Today you work out what the system was actually delivering, put the steps of synchronising a machine in the order physics requires, and settle an argument between a meter and an oscilloscope. This time Farrow is right, and the delay is the cheapest thing in the week: a number in a report outlives everybody who knew what it meant.
A reading is a claim about one quantity, and two instruments can disagree while both are right.
What three phases actually add up to
Estimate the power the circuit was delivering
Metering & Standards
Farrow has line voltage, line current and a power factor from the night of the event. The report claims a figure for delivered power that nobody has reproduced.
Three-phase power from line quantities carries a factor of root three, and it is not three.
a three-phase supply carries power on three conductors at once
Estimate the real power the circuit was delivering.

The tempting mistake is to multiply by three, because there are three phases. The factor is the square root of three instead, and the reason is that line voltage is measured between two phases rather than from one phase to neutral. Those two ways of measuring differ by root three, and the formula written in line quantities carries it. Power factor then takes its usual bite, because only the in-phase part of the current does work. Get the factor wrong and the answer is out by about seventy per cent, which is more than enough to change what the report concludes.
The circuit was at 11,000 V between lines, carrying 310 A per line, at 0.95 power factor. Root three is about 1.732.
Choose root three, the line voltage, the line current and the power factor.

About five and a half megawatts. Using three instead of root three gives nearly ten, which is a different circuit. The phase count is a real fact about the system and is not the multiplier here. Sin φ belongs to the reactive part, which is a separate question.
Real power = √3 × the line voltage × the line current × the power factor, with the voltage measured between lines rather than to neutral.
Line voltage is 11,000 V and line current is 310 A
Power factor is 0.95
Root three is about 1.732
Four things that have to agree before the breaker closes
Put the steps of synchronising in the order physics requires
Generation Hall
Haddad has a machine at rest and a system running at nominal. She wants the sequence written down before anybody is standing at the panel.
Speed, then voltage, then phase angle, and only then the breaker.
a generator joined to a live system is forced to turn at the system's speed

Each step removes one way of getting hurt, and the order is set by how violent the mismatch is. Speed comes first, because closing onto a system turning at a different rate slams the rotor into step and can shear a shaft. Voltage next, because a difference in size drives a heavy current of reactive power the instant the contacts meet. Phase angle after that, since it is the last thing left and the one that has to be caught in a narrow window as the two drift past each other. The breaker closes last, on all three conditions at once, which is the only moment it is safe.
Bring the machine up to the system's frequency.
Match the machine's voltage to the system's.
Wait for the phase angle between them to close on zero.
Close the breaker.
Two instruments, two quantities
Settle the argument between the meter and the scope
Transmission & Protection
An oscilloscope on the busbar shows a peak of 325 volts. The panel meter beside it reads 230. Both were calibrated last month and neither has moved.
Peak and RMS are different quantities, and one is the other divided by root two.
an alternating voltage changes continuously through each cycle
Which instrument is reporting the wrong voltage?

An alternating voltage does not have one value, so any single number is a summary and the summary has to be named. The peak is the highest the waveform reaches. The RMS value is the steady voltage that would deliver the same power into a resistance, and for a sine wave it is the peak divided by root two. Divide 325 by 1.414 and the meter's 230 comes straight out. This is why mains voltages are quoted as RMS everywhere: it is the figure that predicts heating and power. The peak still matters, but it matters to insulation rather than to power.
The oscilloscope, because 325 volts is not a voltage this system runs at.
Neither, since the scope shows peak and the meter shows RMS.
The meter, because it is averaging and averaging loses the true value.
Both, because two instruments this far apart cannot both be calibrated.
325 volts is exactly what a 230 volt RMS supply peaks at, so it is the expected figure, not an impossible one.
